st_story_blurb: Follow Asha, a Class 11 student in Hyderabad, as she saves for a laptop and the Youth Innovation Fair.
st_locked: Finish the earlier chapter first. Each chapter continues Asha's story.
st_practice_note: Practice replay: Asha's saved story and money are not changed.
st_diary_entry: Dear diary, here is where my money stands.
st_chapter_done: Chapter complete! Asha's diary is saved.
st_story_done: The whole diary is written. Well played!
st_stars_note: Stars are for careful decisions, not for having the most money.
st_sorted_some: Some needed a second look. That is how learning works.
end_fair: Asha and Ravi showed their water-saving app at the Youth Innovation Fair.
end_lite: She presented on the refurbished Lite.
end_wait: She presented on the school lab laptop and is still saving for her own.
end_debt: She still owes ₹{debt} on store credit and pays ₹{plan} a month to clear it.
end_scam_learned: A fake message once cost her money. Now she stops, checks and reports.
end_scam_safe: No fake message got a single rupee from her.
wrap_debt: Still owed on store credit: ₹{debt} (plan: ₹{plan} a month)
c1_summary: Plan a week of pocket money: needs, wants and what is left.
c1_a1: Asha, here is ₹1,000 for the week. It has to cover your bus, lunch and phone recharge.
c1_a2: Thank you, Amma! This time I will plan it properly.
c1_a3: Ms. Farida announced the Youth Innovation Fair today. Ravi and I want to build a water-saving app.
c1_a4: But we need a laptop, and laptops cost a lot.
c1_a5: We cannot buy one right now. Save what you can. Every rupee you keep aside is a start.
c1_a6: I'm Gullu, your gullak! Plan the week first. Whatever is left comes to me.
c1_budget_intro: Tap things to add them to this week's plan. Tap again to take them out. Watch what is left.
c1_over: This plan is ₹{over} more than Asha has. Take something out.
c1_missing_bus: No bus pass means a 4 km walk each way and being late for class. Needs come first.
c1_missing_lunch: Without lunch money Asha will be hungry all week. Needs come first.
c1_missing_recharge: Without a recharge Asha misses the fair group's messages. Needs come first.
c1_b_zero: I have planned every rupee. Nothing is left if something comes up.
c1_b_movie: Movie on Saturday! I'm glad you kept room for it.
c1_b_none: No movie, no chaat? You are serious about that laptop! Maybe plan one small treat next week.
c1_b_phones: The headphones are great for online classes. But they took a big bite out of the week.
c1_b_form: Fair registration forms are out. Printing and photocopies cost ₹60. Hand them in by Friday.
c1_form_prompt: A surprise ₹60. How will Asha pay?
c1_form_own: Pay from the money I kept aside
c1_form_own_r: Asha paid ₹60 from what she had kept aside. That is what leftover money is for: surprises.
c1_form_advance: Ask Amma for ₹60 from next week's money
c1_form_advance_r: Amma agrees, but next week's money will be ₹60 less. An advance is borrowing from your future self.
c1_form_skip_r: No form, no fair. And the fair is the whole plan. Find another way to pay.
c1_sort_intro: I am writing the week in my money diary. Was each thing a need or a want?
c1_why_bus: Getting to class is a need.
c1_why_recharge: Asha needs her phone for class and fair messages, so this recharge is a need.
c1_why_movie: Fun, but the week works without it. A want.
c1_why_headphones: Useful, but Asha can study without them. A want.
c1_why_chaat: A treat with friends is a want.
c1_why_form: The form is needed to enter the fair.
c1_teach_1: A budget is a plan for your money, made before you spend it.
c1_teach_2: Needs come first. Wants are fine when they fit.
c1_teach_3: Opportunity cost: choosing one thing means giving up another.
c1_teach_4: Money kept aside is what handles surprises.
c2_summary: Pick a savings target and save a little every week.
c2_a1: Asha, we talked it over. If you save ₹3,000 as your share, Amma and I will add the rest for a laptop.
c2_a2: Really? I have ₹{jar} in my gullak now. Ammamma's ₹100 gift is already in there.
c2_a3: Big target! My brother says: start with a smaller goal so you don't give up.
c2_a4: Good advice. Pick a first target, then save a little every week.
c2_goal_intro: Which target should I save for first?
c2_goal_try: If I save this much each week:
c2_b1: Each week Asha gets ₹300. Decide how much comes to me and how much she spends.
c2_b_advance: Remember the ₹60 advance? I have kept it back from this week's money.
c2_week_intro: Week {n}: ₹{income} to decide about. How much goes into the gullak?
c2_eta_never: Saving nothing this week: the target comes no closer.
c2_eta: At ₹{weekly} a week: about {weeks} more weeks
c2_note_advance: ₹{cost} went back to Amma for last week's advance.
c2_note_treat: ₹{cost} is already spent on Ravi's birthday.
c2_note_lab: ₹{cost} is already paid for the lab record book.
c2_c1: It's my birthday on Friday! Everyone is going for biryani, ₹100 each. Are you coming?
c2_treat_prompt: Ravi's birthday or the savings target?
c2_treat_join_r: Asha had a great evening with her friends. ₹100 of this week's money is spent, so there is less to save. Enjoying money you planned for is not a mistake.
c2_treat_small: Suggest samosas and a handmade card (₹30)
c2_treat_small_r: Ravi loved the card. ₹30 spent, and the friendship is just fine. A cheaper plan can still be fun.
c2_treat_skip: Skip it and save the money
c2_treat_skip_r: Asha kept the full amount, but missed the party. Saving matters, and so do friends. Only you can balance the two.
c2_d1: Class, the lab record book is compulsory this week. It costs ₹80.
c2_d2: A need, not a want. It comes out first.
c2_teach_1: A goal with a number is easier to reach than a wish.
c2_teach_2: Saving a little regularly beats saving a lot once.
c2_teach_3: Delayed gratification: waiting now to get something better later.
c2_teach_4: Plan for needs that compete with your goal.
c3_summary: Open a bank account, pay by UPI and handle a pending payment.
c3_a1: Your gullak is getting heavy! Time to open a student savings account at Charminar Sahakari Bank.
c3_a2: Welcome, Asha. I'm Lakshmi. A bank keeps your money safe and records every rupee in and out.
c3_a3: I will add ₹200 to start your account.
c3_a4: One rule before we begin: your UPI PIN and OTP are secret. Even I will never ask for them.
c3_open_intro: Move the gullak money into your new account.
c3_b1: Here is your pretend banking app. Try three things: deposit this week's ₹300, withdraw ₹200 in cash, and pay Imran bhai ₹150 by UPI for project printouts.
c3_bank_intro: Pick an action, choose the amount and confirm. Watch the balance change.
c3_check_intro: Now check your passbook. One balance is hidden. What should it be?
c3_task_upi: Pay ₹150 by UPI to Imran Stationery
c3_pin_note: The game enters a pretend PIN for you. Never type or tell anyone your real UPI PIN.
c3_hint_done: That task is already done. Look at the list for what is left.
c3_hint_amount: Check the amount against the task list.
c3_hint_payee: Check who you are paying. Money sent to the wrong person is hard to get back.
c3_check_q: What should the balance be after the last line?
c3_check_why: ₹{start} + 300 − 200 − 150 = ₹{end}. Checking the history yourself catches mistakes.
c3_c1: The fair entry fee is ₹100. Pay it by UPI to the Fair Desk.
c3_pending_intro: Scan the Fair Desk code and pay ₹100.
c3_pending_think: It did not say success. What should I do?
c3_pending_after: So that is what happened to my ₹100.
c3_pending_body: The app is still waiting for the bank's reply. Reference FD7731.
c3_pend_cash: Pay ₹100 in cash at the desk instead
c3_history_tap: Tap the payment to see its status.
c3_detail: Status: Pending. ₹100 is on hold from your balance. It will either reach the Fair Desk or come back to you. Paying again now could mean paying twice.
c3_res_verify: The payment went through. The Fair Desk has ₹100 and Asha paid exactly once.
c3_res_double: Both payments went through, so ₹200 left the account. The Fair Desk returned the extra ₹100 in cash. Not every receiver will.
c3_res_cash: Asha paid cash, and then the UPI payment also went through. The Fair Desk returned the extra ₹100 in cash. Not every receiver will.
c3_d_verify: You checked before paying again. A pending payment is not a failed payment. The money may already be on its way.
c3_d_double: Asha, we got ₹100 from you twice! Here is ₹100 back in cash.
c3_d_cash: Your UPI payment arrived too, so you paid twice. Here is your ₹100 cash back.
c3_d_lesson: Lucky the Fair Desk was honest. Always check the status before paying again.
c3_teach_1: A deposit adds to your balance. Withdrawals and payments reduce it.
c3_teach_2: The transaction history shows whether a payment really went through.
c3_teach_3: Pending means wait and check. Do not pay again straight away.
c3_teach_4: Never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone.
c4_summary: Investigate four messages and decide which ones to trust.
c4_a1: My laptop fund is growing slowly. Maybe a scholarship could help. Let me search.
c4_a2: Careful. When you look for money online, tricksters look for you.
c4_inbox_intro: Open each message. Tap any part that looks wrong, then decide what Asha does.
c4_inbox_done: All four handled. Let's see what happened.
c4_msg_intro: Hmm. Which parts of this look odd?
c4_no_clue: Nothing odd in that part. Look again.
c4_do_verify: Check first with someone I trust
c4_res_ok: Safe, but the sender is still out there
c4_m1_s0: Congratulations! Your number has won ₹25,000 in the Lucky Student Draw.
c4_m1_s1: To receive it, reply with the OTP we just sent to your phone.
c4_m1_s2: Hurry! The offer ends in 10 minutes.
c4_m1_k1: An OTP is a key to your money. Nobody honest asks for it.
c4_m1_k2: Rushing you is a pressure trick.
c4_m1_do: Reply with the OTP to claim the prize
c4_m1_safe: There was no prize. The OTP would have approved a payment out of Asha's account.
c4_m1_ignore: Nothing lost. Reporting the sender would also protect other students.
c4_m1_proceed: The OTP approved a payment. ₹{loss} left Asha's pretend account in seconds.
c4_m2_s0: Hello, I am the manager of Charminar Sahakari Bank, messaging from my personal number.
c4_m2_s1: Your account will be blocked today.
c4_m2_s2: Send your UPI PIN now to keep it active.
c4_m2_k0: A bank does not message from a personal number.
c4_m2_k1: A threat with a deadline is meant to scare you.
c4_m2_k2: No bank employee ever needs your PIN.
c4_m2_do: Send the UPI PIN to keep the account open
c4_m2_safe: Lakshmi ma'am confirms it: the bank never asks for a PIN. The account was never in danger.
c4_m2_ignore: Nothing lost. Calling the bank's official number would have warned them about the impostor.
c4_m2_proceed: With the PIN, the impostor moved ₹{loss} out of Asha's pretend account.
c4_m3_s0: Vidya Jyoti Scholarship: ₹50,000 for Class 11 students.
c4_m3_s1: You are already selected. No marks or documents needed.
c4_m3_s2: Pay a ₹499 processing fee today to confirm your seat.
c4_m3_k1: Selected without applying? Too good to be true.
c4_m3_k2: Real scholarships do not charge a fee to give you money.
c4_m3_k3: A strange web address, not an official one.
c4_m3_safe: There is no such scholarship. The fee was the whole point of the message.
c4_m3_ignore: Nothing lost. Asking Ms. Farida would also have pointed Asha to real, free scholarships.
c4_m3_proceed: ₹{loss} left Asha's pretend account. No scholarship ever arrived.
c4_m4_s0: Hi Asha, it's Ravi. This is my new number.
c4_m4_s2: Send it to UPI ID rk.store77. Don't call, I'm in class.
c4_m4_k0: A new number: anyone can claim to be Ravi.
c4_m4_k1: Urgent money requests are a common trick.
c4_m4_k2: A shop-like UPI ID, and "don't call" stops you from checking.
c4_m4_safe: The real Ravi never sent it. Someone was pretending to be him.
c4_m4_ignore: Nothing lost. But if it had been real, Ravi would have needed help. Calling his old number settles it.
c4_m4_proceed: ₹{loss} went to a stranger's account. It was not Ravi at all.
c4_recover_intro: Asha, money has left your account! Quick, what do we do?
c4_recover_after: You told us straight away. That is what saved most of it.
c4_recover_pick: Pick the three actions that help.
c4_rec_wait: Wait a few days and hope it sorts itself out
c4_rec_tell: Tell Amma and Nanna right now
c4_rec_reply: Message the sender and ask for the money back
c4_rec_bank: Call the bank's official number to block payments
c4_rec_report: Report it on the cyber-crime helpline 1930
c4_recover_wrong: Not quite. Waiting loses time, and talking to the trickster gives them another chance.
c4_recover_done: Because Asha acted fast, ₹{back} was stopped and returned. ₹{gone} could not be recovered. In real life, speed matters and not everything comes back.
c4_b_ravi_safe: That wasn't me! Someone copied my photo. Thanks for calling first. I have warned the others.
c4_b_ravi_unsafe: Asha, I never asked for money! That was a fake account. Next time, call me on my real number.
c4_b_farida: Real scholarships never ask for a fee. I will show you the official portal at school. It is free.
c4_b_amma: Reporting quickly brought back ₹{c4_back}. ₹{c4_gone} is gone for good. I am glad you told us.
c4_b_clean: Four messages, zero rupees lost. You stopped, checked and stayed safe.
c4_rules_intro: Quick check before bed: what is safe to share?
c4_card_upiid: Your UPI ID, so a friend can pay you
c4_card_fair: The date of the Innovation Fair
c4_why_otp: An OTP approves a payment. It is only for you.
c4_why_upiid: A UPI ID only lets people send you money.
c4_why_pin: The PIN unlocks your account. Never tell anyone.
c4_why_cvv: The CVV lets someone pay with the card.
c4_why_fair: Public information is fine to share.
c4_teach_1: Never share an OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone.
c4_teach_2: Urgency, surprise prizes and fees up front are warning signs.
c4_teach_3: Verify through a number or website you already trust.
c4_teach_4: If it goes wrong: tell a trusted adult, call the bank, report to 1930.
c5_summary: Compare saving, a cheaper laptop and store credit.
c5_a1: Asha! Looking for a laptop for the fair? I have two that students like.
c5_a2: The Nova 14: your share is ₹3,000. Or the refurbished Lite: older, but it runs your project. Your share is ₹1,200.
c5_a3: I have ₹{bank} in the bank and ₹{wallet} in cash.
c5_a4: There is also EasyPay store credit: take it today, pay later. But read the terms first.
c5_a5: Borrowed money is not your money. Look at all three options before you choose.
c5_shop_intro: Tap each option to inspect it. Then choose.
c5_opt_wait_d: Buy nothing today. Use the school lab laptop for the fair.
c5_opt_lite_d: Older and slower, but enough for the project.
c5_opt_nova_d: The laptop Asha has been saving for.
c5_wait_note: At ₹{habit} saved each month, the full share is about {months} months away.
c5_short_by: Your own money is short by
c5_credit_note: On store credit, paying only the minimum of ₹{min} a month takes {months} months and costs ₹{total} in all: ₹{interest} more than the price.
c5_pay_intro: How would you like to pay?
c5_prev_debit: ₹{price} leaves the bank right away. ₹{after} stays. Nothing to repay.
c5_prev_cash: ₹{price} leaves the wallet right away. ₹{after} stays. Nothing to repay.
c5_prev_credit: Asha takes the laptop today and owes ₹{price}. Her savings stay, but a statement comes every month until it is repaid.
c5_b_wait1: No laptop yet? You can book the school lab laptop for the fair, two hours a day.
c5_b_wait2: That works. I will keep saving.
c5_b_own: It's mine, and paid in full. Nothing to repay!
c5_b_credit: It's yours today. Here is your first statement. The money is borrowed until you repay it.
c5_b_sample: Curious about credit? Here is a sample statement, so you know how it works before you ever need it.
c5_stmt_intro: Read your statement, then choose what to pay this month.
c5_stmt_sample: This is only a sample. Explore it. Nothing here is owed.
c5_stmt_rule: Pretend rule: pay everything by the due date and there is no interest. Whatever is left unpaid grows by 3% every month.
c5_stmt_q: If only the minimum of ₹{min} is paid each month, how much is paid back in all for ₹{owed}?
c5_stmt_q_why: It takes {months} months and ₹{total} in all. ₹{interest} of that is interest: the price of borrowing.
c5_sim_legend: The bar shows how much of the repayment is the laptop. The empty part is interest.
c5_pay_now_q: Asha has ₹{bank} in the bank. What does she pay now?
c5_teach_1: Cash and debit use your own money. Credit is borrowed money.
c5_teach_2: A statement shows what you owe, the due date and the minimum payment.
c5_teach_3: Paying only the minimum costs more: interest is added to what is left.
c5_teach_4: Before borrowing, ask: can I repay it, and what will it cost in total?
c5_wrap_wait: Laptop: the school lab laptop for now
c6_summary: Compare a savings account and a fixed deposit over six months.
c6_a1: Asha, your money can earn while it waits. Keep it in the savings account at 3% a year, or lock some in a fixed deposit at 6% a year for six months.
c6_a2: 6% is double! Why would anyone choose 3%?
c6_a3: Because money in a fixed deposit is locked. Break it early and, at this bank, you get no interest on it.
c6_a4: These rates are made up for the game. Real rates change and are never a promise.
c6_compare_intro: Guess first, then move the months forward and watch.
c6_assume: Example only: ₹{amount} in each, simple interest, made-up rates. Not a promise of real returns.
c6_q: After six months, how much more interest does the fixed deposit earn on ₹{amount}?
c6_try_sav: No problem. Savings-account money can be used any day, and the rest keeps earning.
c6_try_fd: The deposit would have to be broken. At this pretend bank that means no interest on it at all.
c6_try_fd_done: The six months are over, so the deposit and its interest are free to use.
c6_q_why: Savings account: ₹{sav}. Fixed deposit: ₹{fd}. The deposit earns ₹{diff} more, but only if it stays locked.
c6_fd_intro: How much of my ₹{bank} should I lock away for six months?
c6_fd_proj: If it stays locked, this deposit earns about ₹{interest} in six months.
c6_low_cushion: Very little would stay within reach if something unexpected came up. It is still your choice.
c6_b1: Let's move time forward. Each month Asha adds ₹{habit} from her pocket money.
c6_b_debt: The store credit also takes ₹{plan} each month, plus interest on what is still owed.
c6_time_intro: Tap to move to the next month.
c6_event_intro: Asha! Our demo board burnt out. We need ₹300 for new parts today.
c6_time_end: Six months are up. Here is what the money did.
c6_event_body: The fair prototype needs new parts: ₹{cost}, today. The fixed deposit matures only in month 6.
c6_evt_savings_no: Pay from the savings account (not enough there)
c6_evt_savings_r: Paid from money within reach. The fixed deposit keeps earning.
c6_evt_break_no: Break the fixed deposit (there is none)
c6_evt_break_r: The deposit money came back and paid the bill, but it earned no interest.
c6_evt_family: Ask Amma for ₹300 and repay her in month 6
c6_evt_family_r: Amma lent ₹300. Asha's own money was untouched, and she will repay it when the six months end.
c6_time_start: Month 0. Asha's money is in place. Step through the next six months.
c6_c_savings: You kept enough outside the deposit, so the surprise did not touch it.
c6_c_break: Breaking the deposit paid the bill, but its interest was lost. A cushion outside the deposit would have saved it.
c6_c_family: I am glad you asked. And you paid me back when the six months were over.
c6_teach_1: Interest is what a bank pays you for keeping money with it.
c6_teach_2: A higher rate usually comes with a condition, like locking the money.
c6_teach_3: Liquidity means how quickly you can use your money.
c6_teach_4: Keep a cushion within reach before you lock the rest. Rates here are examples, not promises.
c7_summary: Handle a family emergency and read an insurance policy.
c7_a1: One week to the fair! Our app demo is almost ready.
c7_a2: Asha, Nanna slipped at work and hurt his wrist. The clinic bill is ₹1,000.
c7_a3: It is only a sprain. But the bill has to be paid this week, and this month's budget is already tight.
c7_a4: We have a health policy, don't we? Maybe it pays.
c7_a5: Maybe. Read what the policy covers before you count on it.
c7_policy_intro: Tap each part of the policy to read it.
c7_policy_q2_intro: Now one more, to be sure you can read a policy.
c7_pol_premium_b: ₹150 every month. The family pays this whether or not anyone falls ill.
c7_pol_limit_b: Pays up to ₹20,000 in a year for hospital stays.
c7_pol_deductible_b: The family pays the first ₹500 of every claim. The policy pays the rest, up to the limit.
c7_pol_exclusions_b: Not covered: clinic visits without a hospital stay, and medicines bought outside.
c7_pol_covered_b: A two-day hospital stay for dengue costs ₹8,000. The policy pays ₹7,500 and the family pays ₹500.
c7_pol_excluded_b: A clinic visit and bandage for a sprain cost ₹700. The policy pays nothing.
c7_read_more: Read at least {n} parts before deciding.
c7_q1: Will this policy pay today's ₹1,000 clinic bill?
c7_q1_yes_r: The claim came back unpaid. A clinic visit without a hospital stay is in the exclusions. Having insurance does not mean every bill is paid.
c7_q1_no_r: Right. A clinic visit without a hospital stay is excluded, so the family must find the ₹1,000 itself.
c7_q2: If Nanna had needed a hospital stay costing ₹{bill}, how much would the policy pay?
c7_q2_why: A hospital stay is covered. The family pays the ₹{own} deductible and the policy pays ₹{pays} of the ₹{bill}.
c7_b_tried: The claim came back: not covered. Clinic visits are in the exclusions. We should have read it first.
c7_b_right: You are right. It covers hospital stays, not clinic visits. Good that we checked before counting on it.
c7_b_addon: The agent offers an add-on: ₹100 more each month, and clinic visits are covered up to ₹2,000 a year. What do you think, Asha?
c7_addon_prompt: What should the family do about the policy?
c7_addon_keep: Keep the policy as it is (₹150 a month)
c7_addon_keep_r: The family stays protected against a big hospital bill and handles small costs from its emergency fund. A reasonable balance.
c7_addon_add: Add clinic cover (₹250 a month in total)
c7_addon_add_r: Clinic visits are now covered up to ₹2,000 a year, for ₹1,200 more a year. Worth it only if the family visits the clinic often and can afford the premium.
c7_addon_drop: Cancel the policy and save ₹150 a month
c7_addon_drop_r: The family saves ₹1,800 a year. But one hospital stay like the ₹8,000 example would then be paid in full. That is a big risk for a small saving.
c7_c1: Now, the ₹1,000. Let's look at this month's money together.
c7_plan_intro: Tap where the money should come from until the bill is covered.
c7_plan_ready: That covers it. Shall we pay the clinic?
c7_extra: ₹{extra} extra stays in the family budget.
c7_src_fund_d: Money kept aside for exactly this.
c7_src_tv: Pause the TV pack for a month
c7_src_tv_d: A want. It can come back next month.
c7_src_uncle: Borrow from Mama, repay next month
c7_src_uncle_d: Family help, with a clear plan to return it.
c7_src_food: Cut the rice and dal money
c7_warn_power: An unpaid electricity bill brings a late fee and a power cut. Cut wants before needs.
c7_warn_food: Food for the month is a need. Cut wants before needs.
c7_src_asha_d: Her choice. It is her laptop money.
c7_d1: Welcome to the Youth Innovation Fair! Team Asha and Ravi, you are up.
c7_d_nova: Our demo runs on the Nova. It is smooth!
c7_d_lite: The Lite is old, but it runs our app perfectly.
c7_d_wait: We booked the lab laptop and practised in every slot we got.
c7_d_debt: I still owe ₹{debt} on the store credit. I will keep paying ₹{plan} every month until it is cleared.
c7_d_share: You have saved your full share, Asha. Let's go and choose that laptop together.
c7_d_uncle: We will return Mama's ₹300 next month, as promised.
c7_d3: My wrist is fine, the bill is paid, and you handled it like a grown-up.
c7_d4: From ₹1,000 of pocket money to here. Plans changed, and you changed with them. That is what managing money means.
c7_teach_1: An emergency fund is money kept ready for surprises.
c7_teach_2: Insurance covers some risks, not all. Read the limit, the deductible and the exclusions.
c7_teach_3: A premium is the price of protection. It has to fit the budget.
